title: Building a purpose-built small model: the prework
voice:
Write as Avinash Gosavi, a staff engineer who leads a networking platform team and builds side projects on weekends.
- First person, plain and direct. Short declarative sentences mixed with a longer explanatory one. No hype, no marketing words.
- Opens with the concrete situation, then the reasoning. Headings are conversational ("What we actually did"), not clever.
- Opinionated but shows the trade-off. Says "I think" or "my read" when it's a judgment, states facts flatly when they're facts.
- Favors paragraphs over bullet lists; uses a list only for truly parallel items. Uses em-dashes sparingly for clarification.
- Specific numbers and names over adjectives. Dry rather than jokey.
- Sample of his prose: "In the old world, this kind of cleanup almost never happens on schedule. It's not that people don't want to do it. It's that the cost is high." / "The days of 'I can't afford to run this side project' are over. The only cost now is your time."
Rules for phrasing: keep the writer's own words and phrasings wherever they appear in the notes; only reorder, connect and tidy. Never add a fact, number or claim that is not in the notes or the reference facts. If the notes are thin, write less rather than padding. No intro like "In this post"; no summary paragraph at the end unless the notes have one.

sections.name: Why a small model
sections.facts:
- Project: open-source small model that turns a plain-English intent into a correct device config; Cisco first; vendor-neutral via OpenConfig YANG.
- Deterministic, auditable, runs locally; built in public under your name.
questions: What's the one-line pitch for the model? Say it the way you'd say it to a teammate.
What annoyed you about using a big general LLM for network config? Any specific moment?
Why do you want this to run on-prem / on the box rather than via an API?
What do you personally want out of this project (learning, name on it, open source)?
What are the four questions this post answers, in your words?

sections.name: Sourcing the data
sections.facts:
- No public corpus of real configs. NANOG 2022 'dump of NOS config examples' thread -> only Jerikan generated configs (https://lists.nanog.org/archives/list/test@lists.nanog.org/thread/JT5MQ4CVDSL777DL6CSQW7LPEEO6BUOR). HF: one 750-row Cisco command dataset. GitHub configs mostly unlicensed (view/fork only per GitHub ToS).
- MITRE T1602.002: config dumps leak topology and credentials (https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1602/002/).
- arXiv 2512.02861: ~10k intent->config pairs mined from Cisco IOS XE 16.11.1 config-guide PDFs; LLM wrote the matching requirement (https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.02861).
- Validators: ciscoconfparse2 (syntax), Batfish (Apache 2.0, semantics; Cisco/Juniper/Arista...), containerlab or Cisco Modeling Labs (emulation).
- NetConfArena (arXiv 2608.23179): 96 templates -> 480 tasks, validated in GNS3; qwen3-8B scored 4.6-9.4%.
- Dataset size: LIMA 1k curated > 52k; LIMIT 1k-6k useful; practitioner estimate 10k-19k for networking (jaredwatkins.com).
- Plan: ~5k validated config-generation pairs first, OpenConfig YANG as intent format.
questions: Where did you first go looking for real configs, and what did you find?
Why won't network engineers share configs? Have you seen this at work?
How do you plan to generate training pairs? What's the input format, what's the output?
Describe your validation ladder in your own words: parse → Batfish → emulate. Why that order?
How many examples do you think you need, and what's your gut based on?

sections.name: How small can it be
sections.facts:
- Qwen3 pretrained on 36T tokens; TinyLlama 1.1B took 16xA100 for 90 days (https://github.com/jzhang38/TinyLlama).
- Shortlist: Gemma 3 270M (Gemma terms), Qwen3-0.6B/1.7B/4B-Base (Apache 2.0, 32K ctx), SmolLM3-3B (Apache 2.0, 64K), Gemma 4 E4B (Apache 2.0, 128K, 8B on disk).
- arXiv 2512.02861: 7B fine-tune -> 57% fully correct + 38% partial vs 42%/12% general LLM.
- arXiv 2501.19085: fine-tuning helped most at 1B for DSLs (Racket 7%->18%), hurt at 33B.
- arXiv 2507.10182: 7B coder on 1,500 examples matched GPT-4o on spec generation.
- Google pitches Gemma 3 270M for unstructured->structured fine-tunes.
- Q4 sizes (Ollama): Qwen3 0.6B 523MB, 1.7B 1.4GB, 4B 2.6GB, 8B 5.2GB.
questions: When did you realise nobody trains from scratch at hobby scale? What changed in your head?
Which base models are on your shortlist and why those (license? code ability? size)?
Do you think a config is more like code or more like prose? Why does that matter for model size?
What accuracy number would make you comfortable publishing? What's 'good enough'?
What's your experiment plan: start big and step down, or start small?

sections.name: What training costs
sections.facts:
- LoRA: freeze base, train low-rank matrices beside each layer (HF PEFT). QLoRA keeps frozen base in 4-bit.
- Unsloth minimums: QLoRA 3B 3.5GB, 7B 5GB, 8B 6GB VRAM. Full FT 8B: 60-100GB (jarvislabs).
- RunPod (3 Oct 2026): RTX 4090 $0.74/hr, A100 80GB $1.59/hr, H100 $2.89-3.49/hr. Lambda: A100 $2.79, H100 $3.99.
- Worked example: QLoRA 7B for ~$3 in 2-4h on an A100 (dev.to/sebuzdugan).
- Estimates: QLoRA 4B, 10k examples x 3 epochs: 2-4h on 4090, ~$2-3. Full FT 8B ~$10-20. Pretrain 1.1B ~35k GPU-h ~$55k.
- Mac: mlx-lm LoRA/QLoRA, ~250 tok/s for 7B LoRA on M1 Max; 10k x 300 tok x 3 epochs ~8-10h.
- AMD ROCm training on Ryzen AI: possible but rough; Vulkan is inference-only.
- Tools: Unsloth, TRL SFTTrainer, Axolotl, mlx-lm.
questions: What did you assume training would cost before you looked? What's the actual number?
Explain LoRA/QLoRA the way you'd explain it to a Rails engineer.
Which hardware do you own that you'll try first (Mac? the Minisforum?), and what do you expect to go wrong?
Where does the real cost go if not the GPU?
Which tools are you going to use and why?

sections.name: Publishing a model
sections.facts:
- HF Hub repo: .safetensors (pickle gets flagged), tokenizer, chat template, README.md with YAML: license, base_model, datasets, pipeline_tag, model-index. Free public storage best-effort; 4B bf16 ~8GB.
- Qwen3 Apache 2.0 -> your fine-tune can be Apache 2.0 with notice. Gemma derivatives must ship Gemma Terms + NOTICE + use restrictions (also for synthetic-data-trained models). Llama derivatives: 'Llama' in name + 'Built with Meta Llama'.
- Export: merge_and_unload into bf16 base (not the 4-bit one) -> convert_hf_to_gguf.py -> llama-quantize Q4_K_M / Q8_0 -> upload '-GGUF' repo -> `ollama run hf.co/you/model-GGUF`; or Modelfile + `ollama push`.
- Evals before publish: held-out split; task validity benchmark (parses / passes Batfish / boots); lm-evaluation-harness sanity check.
- Dataset repo with dataset card (Parquet); training config + scripts on GitHub, linked from the card.
questions: What did you think 'publishing a model' meant before, and what is it actually?
Which license do you want on your weights, and does your base model let you?
Who do you picture running this, and how (Ollama? llama.cpp? on what box)?
What has to be true before you'd put your name on a release?
Will you publish the dataset and scripts too? Why?

sections.name: So, the plan
sections.facts:
- Milestone 1: a few thousand validated intent->config pairs for everyday Cisco IOS tasks (VLANs, trunks, SVIs, static routes, basic OSPF/BGP), mined from public config guides, checked by ciscoconfparse2 + Batfish.
- Then QLoRA Qwen3-4B-Base on a rented 4090; repeat at 1.7B and 0.6B to find the floor.
- Ship safetensors + GGUF on HF with dataset and scripts.
questions: What changed in your plan after doing this prework?
What's milestone one, concretely? Which config tasks are in scope first?
What will you write about next, and will you include the failures?
